metadata.title: How To Obtain a Covered Product Authorization
metadata.topic: Draft guideline · FDA human drugs and biologics

candidates.statement: developers of potential drug and biological products to obtain samples 3 of brand products 4 that 36 they need to support their applications. CREATES establishes a private right of action that 37 allows eligible product developers 5 to sue brand companies that refuse to sell them product 38 samples needed to support their applications. If the product developer prevails, the court will 39 order the sale of samples, will award attorneys’ fees and litigation costs to the product developer, 40 and may impose a monetary penalty on the brand company. 41 If a product developer is not able to obtain samples of the brand product that they need to support 42 their application from the brand company on a voluntary basis and seeks to use the pathway 43 made available by CREATES, they must take a number of specific steps (outlined in the law) 44 before the brand company will be required to sell them product samples under CREATES. One 45 of these steps – if the brand product for which samples are sought is subject to a Risk Evaluation 46 and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) with elements to assure safe use (ETASU) 6 – is that the product 47 developer must first obtain a Covered Product Authorization (CPA) from FDA (21 U.S.C. 355- 48 2(b)(2)). 7 CREATES does not require this step for products that are not subject to REMS with 49 ETASU. This guidance describes how an eligible product developer can obtain a CPA from 50 FDA. 51
candidates.context: 2 See P.L. 116-94 ( Further Consolidated Appropriations Act , 2020, enacting Division N, Title I, Subtitle F, Section 610—Actions for Delays of Generic Drugs and Biosimilar Biological Products (Dec. 20, 2019)). The provisions of this law related to access to product samples were codified at 21 U.S.C. 355-2 and 355-1(l). A. Relevant Product Types 53

candidates.statement: 6 FDA’s online listing of approved REMS is available at https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cder/rems/index.cfm . Product developers should check this listing to confirm that the product for which they seek a CPA is covered by a REMS with ETASU before submitting a CPA request.
candidates.context: 5 See definitions in section III.A. Note that this guidance also refers to eligible product developers as product developers. 7 Note that requesting or obtaining a CPA from FDA is not a legal requirement to obtain samples of a covered product, and the process described in this guidance is voluntary and applies only to those who seek to avail themselves of the CREATES pathway to obtain such samples. CREATES also provides a pathway for obtaining samples of covered products that are not subject to REMS with ETASU. 21 U.S.C. 355-2.

candidates.statement: Section 505(b)(2) of the FD&C Act represents another abbreviated approval pathway added by 72 the Hatch-Waxman Amendments. As background, a “stand-alone new drug application (NDA)” 73 submitted under section 505(b)(1) contains full reports of investigations of safety and 74 effectiveness that were conducted by or for the applicant or for which the applicant has a right of 75 reference or use (see 21 U.S.C. 355(b)(1), (c)). A “505(b)(2) application,” meanwhile, is an 76 NDA that also contains full reports of investigations of safety and effectiveness, but for which 77 one or more of the investigations relied upon by the applicant for approval “were not conducted 78 by or for the applicant and for which the applicant has not obtained a right of reference or use 79 from the person by or for whom the investigations were conducted” (21 U.S.C. 355(b)(2)). A 80 505(b)(2) application may be submitted to seek approval for, among other things, a new 81 chemical entity, or for a change to an approved drug that would not be permitted under section 82 505(j). A 505(b)(2) application should include, among other things, an identification of those 83 portions of the application that rely on information the applicant does not own or to which the 84 applicant does not have a right of reference. If the 505(b)(2) seeks to rely on the Agency’s 85 previous finding of safety or efficacy for a listed drug, or on literature derived from studies of a 86 listed drug or drugs, a 505(b)(2) application should also include, among other things, a 87 bioavailability/bioequivalence study comparing the proposed product to the listed drug or drugs 88
candidates.context: and studies necessary to support any change or modification from the listed drug or drugs, if any. 89

candidates.statement: The Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act of 2009 (BPCI Act) amended the Public 93 Health Service Act (PHS Act) to create an abbreviated licensure pathway for biological products 94 shown to be biosimilar to, or interchangeable with, an FDA-licensed biological reference product 95 (see sections 7001 through 7003 of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (Public Law 96 111–148)). Section 351(k) of the PHS Act (42 U.S.C. 262(k)), added by the BPCI Act, sets forth 97 the requirements for the licensure of a proposed biosimilar or a proposed interchangeable 98 biosimilar. An application submitted under section 351(k) must contain, among other things, 99 information demonstrating that the biological product is biosimilar to a reference product 8 based 100 upon data derived from analytical studies, animal studies, and a clinical study or studies (see 101 section 351(k)(2)(A)(i)(I) of the PHS Act). FDA has the discretion to determine that an element 102 is unnecessary in a 351(k) application. In addition, FDA expects that applications for 103 interchangeable biosimilars generally will include data from a “switching study” or studies, 104 meaning a clinical study or studies used to determine the impact of alternating or switching 105
candidates.context: 3. Biosimilar Products 91 8 Under section 351(i)(4) of the PHS Act, the term “reference product” means the single biological product licensed under section 351(a) of that Act, against which a biological product is evaluated in a 351(k) application.

candidates.statement: To prevail in the private right of action established by CREATES, the eligible product developer 205 must prove that it has taken a number of specific steps. It must show, among other things, that it 206 submitted a written request to the license holder to purchase sufficient quantities of the covered 207 product, and that the request (1) was sent to a named corporate officer of the license holder, (2) 208 was made by certified/registered mail with return receipt requested, (3) specified an individual 209 point of contact and a means for written and electronic communication with them, and (4) 210 provided a delivery address for samples. 11 The eligible product developer must also prove that 211 the license holder did not deliver sufficient quantities of the covered product on commercially 212 reasonable, market-based terms within 31 days of receiving the request (for non-REMS ETASU 213 products) or (for REMS ETASU products) within 31 days of receiving either the request OR a 214 copy of the Covered Product Authorization (CPA), whichever is later. 12
candidates.context: B. Covered Product Authorizations Under CREATES 203 The CPA is a document obtained by the eligible product developer from FDA. 217 CREATES provides that “[a]n eligible product developer may submit to [FDA] a written 218 request for the eligible product developer to be authorized to obtain sufficient quantities 219 of an individual covered product subject to a REMS with ETASU.” 13 The law requires 220 that FDA must respond to this request within 120 days. 14

candidates.statement: CPAs are only available for products that are subject to a REMS with ETASU. To prevail in the 223 private right of action established by CREATES, an eligible product developer seeking samples 224 of a product that is not subject to a REMS with ETASU does not need to obtain a CPA. 225
candidates.context: In addition, the CPA established by CREATES replaces the “Safety Determination Letter” that 227 FDA had been issuing prior to CREATES as described in the withdrawn draft guidance for 228 industry How to Obtain a Letter from FDA Stating that Bioequivalence Study Protocols Contain 229 Safety Protections Comparable to Applicable REMS for RLD . The purpose of the Safety 230 Determination Letter was to provide RLD sponsors with written assurance that providing 231 samples to a potential applicant would not be considered a violation of their REMS. The CPA 232 provides the same written assurance. Note that unlike Safety Determination Letters, which FDA 233 sent to the RLD sponsor at the prospective ANDA applicant’s request, CREATES provides that 234 the eligible product developer is responsible for providing a copy of the CPA to the applicable 235 license holder. 15
